All of them run on NVIDIA from the V100 / RTX 20 on, and on AMD and Windows (see [What you need](#what-you-need)). DeepSeek's sizes include its Engram tables. The setup also offers unsloth's GGUF and LibertAIDAI's EXL3 quants of DeepSeek, orcarouter's abliterated DeepSeek, Mia-AiLab's EXL3 quant of MiniMax, turboderp's EXL3 quants of GLM, Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next (CYBER-FROST) as its Q5_K_M GGUF and Qwen-3.8-Flash-Next itself as unsloth's UD-IQ2_XS GGUF, both with pictures ([its settings](docs/SETTINGS.md#qwen-38-flash-next-cyber-frost)). **Each model's files, drafters, pictures and options: [docs/MODELS.md](docs/MODELS.md).** ## Quality Maya's quants are made from each model's released weights and measured against the original: - **GLM-5.3 · Maya quants** keep 97.7-99.2% of the FP8 model's zero-shot accuracy and pick its next token 83-90% of the time (Maya-L: 99.2%, 90%). How they're made and measured: [MAYA-S](bench/results/MAYA-S.md), [MAYA-S24](bench/results/MAYA-S24.md), [MAYA-M](bench/results/MAYA-M.md), [MAYA-L](bench/results/MAYA-L.md). - **DeepSeek V4.1 · Maya-S** picks the same next token as the original 92.6% of the time. - **MiniMax M3.1 · Maya-S** picks it 87.6% of the time (the average over its categories). More on each model's card on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/peasantsmith). ## How fast is it? Real machines measured by our users, most with `./maya.sh --bench` (decode: three greedy 256-token answers; prefill: an 8K-token prompt unless the row says otherwise). Share yours: `--bench`, then `--report`, in a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/mw00/project-maya/issues).

A token is about ¾ of a word. The speed holds as a conversation grows, and the first answers after a start are the slowest while the caches fill with what you use. ## Using it - **In the browser:** chat (kept in your browser, with search, pins and folders, per-chat instructions and thinking level, edit and regenerate, HTML previews), a live **Monitor** of the model and your hardware (down to what fills each GPU's memory), a context size and port you can change in Settings, and **Models**: every model set up on this machine, switching to another (Maya starts again with it) and each one's engine settings (context, GPUs, drafting, images, memory), saved into its `maya-.json`. - **Models page:** the catalog lists every Maya model with its size. Download one with a progress bar, load it, unload the running one or delete one - no command line needed. - **Turbo:** one button beside the model's parameters sets the fastest settings for the model (greedy sampling, no thinking, expert skipping, the fastest drafting). It trades some quality for speed; switching it off restores your settings exactly. - **Saved:** the sidebar's Saved line adds up what the model's own API (DeepSeek's, Z.ai's or MiniMax's) would have charged for the same tokens - the prompt Maya reuses from its cache at the API's cached price, DeepSeek's peak hours at its peak price - kept per model in `token-savings.json`; its prices can be changed in **Settings › Savings**. - **Your apps and coding agents:** an OpenAI-compatible API at `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`, and Anthropic's at `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/messages` (Claude Code: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080`). Tool calls are streamed as the model writes them, and a long prompt's reading progress too when a request asks for it (`"return_progress": true`). A web page served from another address can call it too once you allow its address (`"cors_origins"`, [docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md#web-pages-on-another-address)). - **Responses API:** `/v1/responses` supports text/image conversations, streaming, function tool calls, schema-validated output, background tasks with cancellation/replay, and optional shared in-memory history (`store:true`, `previous_response_id`). Responses are not stored by default. Options and limits: [docs/RESPONSES.md](docs/RESPONSES.md). - **Model API:** `/api/tags`, `/api/ps`, `/api/show`, `/api/chat`, `/api/generate`, `/api/pull` and `/api/delete` list, load, download and delete models from any app or script. A request for a model that is not loaded swaps to it, and `keep_alive` unloads it when idle. `/models/load`, `/models/unload` and `/models/sse` are on by default too (`"model_management": false` turns them off). - **Thinking:** Off, Low, High (the default) or Max, in Settings or per request, and a **thinking budget** field that sets how many tokens the model may think before it answers. - **Loop guard:** on by default - an agent that repeats the same tool call with the same result is steered off it. - **Pictures:** attach one in the chat, or send image parts through either API. Every model reads them (setup details per model: [docs/MODELS.md](docs/MODELS.md)). Videos too, for the models that read them. - **Files:** attach any file in the chat. Text and code go in as they are; **PDFs** as their text, or a scanned one's first pages as pictures; Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument, EPUB and RTF files as their text. Anything Maya can't read says why. The same works through the APIs: OpenAI `file` / `input_file` parts and Anthropic `document` blocks (sent inline). poppler, when installed (`sudo apt install poppler-utils`), reads PDFs a little better; it is optional. - **MCP tools:** list MCP servers in the config (`"mcp_servers"`; Claude Desktop's `mcpServers` block works as it is) and the web chat's model can call their tools. A switch in the chat's **+** menu turns them on and off. What it does: [serve/mcp.py](serve/mcp.py). - **Docker:** there is no official image. [docs/DOCKER.md](docs/DOCKER.md) is a recipe to build one from a release. - **From another device:** `./maya.sh --setup --host 0.0.0.0 --api-key `. Always set a key. - **Tuning:** `./maya.sh --calibrate` tunes the engine to your hardware in 10-15 minutes. Every setting: [docs/SETTINGS.md](docs/SETTINGS.md). - **Each model's own options** - GLM-5.3-Flash's several requests at once (`--parallel`), long contexts and DFlash2 drafter; DeepSeek's kept conversations, expert loading and Engram read-ahead; MiniMax's thinking levels: [docs/MODELS.md](docs/MODELS.md). ## What you need | | | | --- | --- | | **GPU** | NVIDIA, compute capability 7.0 or newer (V100, RTX 20 and newer): one, or up to 16 that share the model. More VRAM is faster. Pascal (Tesla P40 / P100, GTX 10) is experimental, not validated yet. **AMD:** RX 7900 XT / XTX, Radeon AI PRO R9700 / RX 9070, Strix Halo and Gorgon Halo (Radeon 8060S / 8065S); RX 6800 / 6900 and Radeon PRO V620 / W6800 not validated yet; GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 read pictures there too - [docs/AMD_MAYA.md](docs/AMD_MAYA.md) | | **RAM** | 32 GB runs it. More RAM keeps more experts close and is faster | | **Disk** | **A fast NVMe SSD** with room for the model (~75 GB for GLM-5.3 · Maya-XS, ~100 GB for GLM-5.3 · Maya-S, ~160 GB for GLM-5.3 · Maya-L, ~350 GB for DeepSeek V4.1 · Maya-S, ~470 GB for unsloth's Q8 GGUF of it, ~95 GB for MiniMax M3.1 · Maya-XS, ~200 GB for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash's EXL3 quant) and its picture encoder (1.1 GB). Not a hard disk | | **System** | Linux (x86-64; a CPU with AVX2 is best), the NVIDIA driver, CUDA 12.x (CUDA 13 works for RTX 20 and newer, not for the V100 or Pascal), g++, Python 3.10+. Windows 10/11: [docs/WINDOWS.md](docs/WINDOWS.md). Not WSL2. AMD: ROCm 7 | The setup checks all of this, prints the exact command for anything missing, and installs nothing system-wide. ## Install Run the two commands in [Quick start](#quick-start) and answer a few questions (Enter takes the recommended choice). The setup shows every download before it starts it, builds everything once (20-40 minutes plus the download) and **starts the model**. Then open `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. Ctrl+C stops it, and `./setup.sh` starts it again right away. - **Windows:** `START-MAYA.bat` instead of `./setup.sh` - see [docs/WINDOWS.md](docs/WINDOWS.md). - **AMD:** [docs/AMD_MAYA.md](docs/AMD_MAYA.md). - **Mac with Apple Silicon (experimental, GLM-5.3-Flash only):** `./maya.sh --backend metal` (on a Mac, `./maya.sh` picks Metal by itself) - see [docs/METAL.md](docs/METAL.md). Built and unit-tested on GitHub's Macs, not yet tested by us with the real model (we have no Mac): if you run it, please tell us how it went in an issue. - **Intel Arc:** not supported by Maya's engine; a community report of the Maya-XS DeepSeek GGUFs on llama.cpp's SYCL backend: [docs/INTEL_ARC.md](docs/INTEL_ARC.md). - **Updating:** the page's **Settings › About and updates**, or `git pull` then `./setup.sh`. The model isn't downloaded again. - **Model files downloaded another way** (a download manager, another PC, a Hugging Face cache): `./maya.sh --import-model FOLDER` finds Maya's files in FOLDER by size and checksum, whatever they are called, and moves them into place (`--copy` when FOLDER is on another drive; the originals stay). Files that do not match are left alone. - **Every option** (GPUs, context, a model folder you already have, remote access, ...): [docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md). > **The start takes a few minutes:** the engine pins most of the free RAM (all but about 6 GB) for its expert tier, > so other programs get little RAM while Maya runs. ## Something went wrong? Run **`./maya.sh --report`** (Windows: `START-MAYA.bat --report`) right after a slow answer or an error, and attach the `maya-report.txt` it writes to a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/mw00/project-maya/issues). It holds your hardware, your setup and the engine's speed lines; nothing is sent anywhere by itself. The engine's own log is `maya-.log` in the Maya folder. - **The build stops** ("nvcc ... cannot build for these GPUs", "unsupported GNU version", or `cuda_profiler_api.h` / `nvtx3/nvToolsExt.h` missing): [docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md#if-the-build-fails) has the fix for each. - **Slow, with the SSD busy all the time:** not enough free RAM for the experts. Close programs or add RAM. - **Windows: answers suddenly several times slower:** the card is too full and Windows moves GPU memory to RAM. Leave more of it free: `START-MAYA.bat --setup --vram-reserve-mib 2048` ([the expert pool's size](docs/SETTINGS.md#the-expert-pools-size)). - **Windows on a Strix Halo / Gorgon Halo: other programs run out of memory, or the setup warns about the page file:** set the page file to the size the setup prints ([docs/AMD_MAYA.md](docs/AMD_MAYA.md)). - **The download stopped:** run `./maya.sh` again; it continues where it stopped. - **Port 8080 is in use:** Maya is already running, or `--port 8081` starts another one. Settings > Port moves Maya to another port for good (it starts again there). ## Support Maya is free and open source, and it always will be. It exists so that anyone can run the biggest open models at home, on hardware they already own. Sponsors make that possible: - **More hardware runs well.** Every release is tested on our own NVIDIA and AMD machines before it ships. Macs are so far tested only on GitHub's virtual Macs. The current goal is 50 monthly sponsors, enough for a real Mac and newer GPUs. - **New models sooner.** Every new model and quant takes many hours of GPU time to build and check. - **Faster fixes** when something breaks on your setup. If you enjoy running big models on your own machine, a small monthly sponsorship is the best way to keep Maya growing. Thank you!

Coding agents load a server differently, and settings that only matter under that load (`--parallel`, the expert tiers, the batched decode, reading a prompt while others decode, keeping a system prompt for the next conversation) show nothing there. `tools/agent_bench.py` runs a scripted agent workload against a running server, so two settings, two builds or two machines can be compared on the same requests. ## What it sends Everything is fixed by `--seed`, so every run sends the same requests: - `--clients` conversations at once (default 4). Each starts with one of a few shared system prompts (30K, 8K and 4K tokens by default) and a first message of 2-6K tokens. - Then turns: each appends new text, as a tool result or a message would, and asks for an answer of 32-1024 tokens. 80% of the new texts are under 2K tokens, 5% are 8K-64K. The next turn comes 2-20 s after the answer (the agent running its tools). - Checks: at `--checks-per-hour` (40), a 30K-token system prompt with a fresh 2-4K-token question and a 16-token answer, as an agent's permission or routing check does. - Two cold bursts, at a third and two thirds of the run: half the conversations start over and are read again with nothing reusable past the system prompt, as after an agent restarts. - A conversation that grows past `--max-context` starts a new one from its latest turn, as an agent compacts. The model's answers are not fed back: the next turn sends the scripted history, so the prompts do not depend on what the model wrote. Requests are greedy with thinking off and ban the model's end tokens (`--ban auto` knows GLM-5.3-Flash by the served model's name; `--ban none` or token ids otherwise), so every answer writes its whole max_tokens and every run writes the same number of tokens. The texts are slices of this repository's files (`--corpus ` for others). ## Running it Start the server the way you use it (`./maya.sh` with your config, `--parallel` as you run it), then: ``` python tools/agent_bench.py run --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 --clients 4 --label mine --out runs/mine-1.json python tools/agent_bench.py plan --clients 4 # what it would send, without a server ``` A run takes `--duration` (900 s) plus the answers in flight. The first `--warmup` seconds (180) are left out of the summary: the server's caches fill with the conversations then. For an A/B, restart the server before each run (a run leaves its conversations in the server's caches), alternate the settings (A B A B), use the same `--seed`, `--clients`, `--duration` and `--warmup`, and run each setting at least twice: ``` python tools/agent_bench.py compare runs/base-*.json runs/new-*.json ``` `compare` prints each metric's mean and standard deviation over a label's runs and marks a difference larger than twice its standard error with `*`. A difference without the mark is within the runs' own spread. It works against any OpenAI-compatible server (the requests are streamed and timed by the client). A Maya server adds its own figures from `GET /metrics`. ## What it reports Over the window from `--warmup` to `--duration` (a request counts when it ends inside it): | metric | what it is | |---|---| | `output_tok_s` | tokens written per second by all conversations together | | `in_flight` | requests in flight on average (with think times, fewer than `--clients`) | | `decode_median`, `decode_p10` | per request: tokens per second from its first token to its last, what an agent sees; slowed by the other conversations' steps and reads (answers of 50 tokens or more) | | `latency_median`, `latency_p90` | a turn from its send to its last token | | `ttft_median`, `ttft_p90` | a turn's time to its first token: the read of its new text and any wait behind other reads | | `decode K+` | the decode median by the request's context length | | `read +` | prompt reads by their number of new tokens (not reused from the server's cache): new tokens per second of read time - the server's own read time when it sends `timings` (Maya, llama.cpp's server), else the time to the first token | | `vram_hit_per_request`, `vram_hit`, `ram_fetch`, `promo` | Maya with experts in RAM: the routed experts found in VRAM per request (median), and the tiers' readings over the run (VRAM hit, RAM-tier experts fetched over PCIe a token, promotions a token) | The run's JSON keeps every request's times, sizes and the server's records, for anything the summary does not show. ## Reading the results - `output_tok_s` follows the workload as much as the server: with think times, a server twice as fast does not write twice as many tokens, because the conversations wait for their tools. Compare `decode_median` and the latencies for speed; `output_tok_s` and `in_flight` show how the load itself moved. - Reads by new tokens and decode by context length compare like with like when runs drift apart (a faster run gets further into its conversations, so its contexts are longer). - With experts in RAM, runs of the same setting differ more than with every expert in VRAM (where experts end up depends on timing): expect a few percent between reps. # RDNA decode expert kernels For `n_embd=4096`, `n_ff=2048`, the HIP decode dispatcher selects kernels by architecture: | Architecture | IQ2_XXS gate/up (`gate_up<16>`) | IQ2_S down (`down<22>`) | IQ3_XXS down (`down<18>`) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | gfx1100 | Optimized | Optimized | Optimized | | gfx1151 | Optimized | Optimized | Original (legacy) | | gfx1201 | Original (legacy) | Original (legacy) | Original (legacy) | gfx1201 is unchanged and untuned by this expert-kernel work. Other shapes, other quant types, other architectures and CUDA keep the original dispatch. Set `MAYA_HIP_EXPERTS_LEGACY=1` before starting a process to force original HIP expert kernels for an end-to-end comparison. The main change is packed sign expansion: a multiply spreads four sign bits into the high bit of four bytes, then masks and shifts produce the XOR masks and two's-complement corrections. Codebook bytes are positive and nonzero, so ordinary word addition introduces no carries between bytes. This replaces HIP's emulated packed compare/subtract while retaining the original integer scale divisions, FP32 accumulation order, clamping, q8_1 quantization and expert combine order. Gate/up retains sixteen wave32 waves per workgroup, two gate and two up rows per wave, its 2 KiB codebook in LDS, and the fused shared-down branch. Down uses two output rows per workgroup instead of four on optimized paths, reducing its register budget. IQ2_S reads its 8 KiB codebook through global memory; IQ3_XXS keeps its 1 KiB codebook in LDS. The grid selection and sign operations are HIP-only. The signed-codebook technique was adapted from [the upstream engine's moe_fused_iq.cu](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/blob/fb58e0dbc8399662c0e47c76578c6e878b14f6cf/src/prefill/moe_fused_iq.cu) (MIT). Its HIP sign lookup tables were measured first; direct sign arithmetic performed better here. The benchmark retains alternatives for reproducible comparison: sign LUTs, global/LDS codebooks, eight/sixteen gate waves, two/four/eight down rows, alignment-safe eight-byte IQ2_XXS/IQ3_XXS quant loads, a separate shared-down launch, and an eight-wave occupancy constraint. Wider loads, splitting shared down, and the occupancy constraint did not beat the selected paths. This work does not fuse gate/up and down into one kernel. ## Reproduce ```bash cmake -S . -B build-multi -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \ -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/rocm-7.2.1 \ -DCMAKE_HIP_COMPILER=/opt/rocm-7.2.1/llvm/bin/clang++ \ -DMAYA_ENABLE_HIP=ON -DMAYA_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF \ -DMAYA_PREFILL_MMQ=ON -DMAYA_NATIVE_EXPERTS=ON \ -DMAYA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF \ -DMAYA_GGML_DIR=/ai/github/project-maya/third_party/llama.cpp \ '-DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1100;gfx1201;gfx1151' CCACHE_DIR=/tmp/maya-experts-ccache cmake --build build-multi -j 8 \ --target maya hip_expert_kernel_bench glm_ffn_parity glm_layer_parity \ glm_model_test iq1_s_parity hip_intrinsics export HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/rocm/lib build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench --shared build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench --parity-only --sweep build-multi/glm_ffn_parity --selftest build-multi/glm_layer_parity --selftest build-multi/glm_model_test --selftest build-multi/iq1_s_parity build-multi/hip_intrinsics ``` Run these commands from the repository root. `--sweep` also works with timing; without it the benchmark compares original kernels against production dispatch. Baseline launches bypass production dispatch, so both implementations are measured in the same binary. `--shared` includes a Q6_K shared-down matrix of shape 4096x2048 in the gate/up launch and a shared contribution in down. Random finite quantized blocks use the actual GGML block layouts (66, 82 and 98 bytes). Eight expert blobs contain `[gate | up | down]`. Timing rotates five independent pools: each kernel's weight working set exceeds the 7900 XT's 80 MiB cache, including down's smaller matrices. Requested weight and buffer allocations are below 300 MiB for either timed fixture. Parity-only uses one pool and less than 80 MiB. Each timing graph contains sixty launches, with seven alternating original/new rounds after warmup. Reported latency is the median graph time per launch. GB/s counts quantized weight bytes (plus shared-down weights with `--shared`), not codebooks, activations or actual DRAM transaction bytes. ## RX 7900 XT results, 2026-10-08 ROCm 7.2.1, Release, all three requested architectures compiled. GPU 0 only; the existing Maya server stayed running. No clocks or other processes were changed. These are synthetic decode measurements, not Strix Halo results. | Kernel | Original us/call | New us/call | Original GB/s | New GB/s | Latency reduction | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | IQ2_XXS gate/up, IQ2_S fixture | 92.572 | 65.607 | 373.80 | 527.43 | 29.1% | | IQ2_S down | 57.806 | 37.570 | 371.86 | 572.15 | 35.0% | | IQ2_XXS gate/up, IQ3_XXS fixture | 93.209 | 68.616 | 371.24 | 504.30 | 26.4% | | IQ3_XXS down | 48.220 | 43.506 | 532.77 | 590.49 | 9.8% | | IQ2_XXS gate/up including shared down, IQ2_S fixture | 101.049 | 77.944 | 410.54 | 532.23 | 22.9% | The full parity sweep passed all 620 comparisons with byte-identical q8_1 outputs and bit-identical FP32 outputs: maximum absolute error and relative L2 were both zero. Cases cover 1/3/8 routed experts, null expert slots, CPU/shared contributions, zero activations, unclamped SwiGLU, and all tuning variants for types 16/18/22. Legacy dispatch parity also passed. All five requested tests passed: `glm_ffn_parity --selftest`, `glm_layer_parity --selftest`, `glm_model_test --selftest`, `iq1_s_parity`, and `hip_intrinsics`. Runtime tests used gfx1100; gfx1151/gfx1201 code objects were built, and gfx1201 continues to select the original kernels. No CUDA toolkit was available for a CUDA build; CUDA retains its original kernel template signatures and arithmetic. Full-model measurements reported after the initial synthetic tests showed decode increasing from 15.1 to 16.4 tok/s (+8.6%) on RX 7900 XT (gfx1100), with bit-identical parity. The two-GPU full-model configuration improved decode by 3.9%. ## Strix Halo 8060S results (gfx1151), 2026-10-08 The following hardware measurements were reported for the original kernels versus the optimized dispatch in commit `6f0bdf6`, before restoring legacy IQ3_XXS down on gfx1151: | Kernel / fixture | Original us/call | Optimized us/call | Speedup | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | `gate_up<16>`, gu16/down22 fixture | 203.9 | 181.4 | 1.124x | | `down<22>` (IQ2_S) | 131.4 | 126.6 | 1.038x | | `gate_up<16>`, gu16/down18 fixture | 207.7 | 183.3 | 1.133x | | `down<18>` (IQ3_XXS) | 126.5 | 130.2 | 0.972x (regression) | Full-model decode on gfx1151 increased from 17.8 to 18.0 tok/s with that dispatch.
